# Empirical Exercise 2.1

## Part A,B and C:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readxl)
library(knitr)

wage_df <- read_excel("C:/Users/dibya/Desktop/Econ 303/Age_HourlyEarnings.xlsx")

# Build joint distribution cleanly
age_df <- wage_df[, -1]
ages <- as.numeric(age_df[1, ])

# Convert joint prob table to numeric safely
joint <- as.data.frame(age_df[-1, ])
joint[] <- lapply(joint, as.numeric)
joint_mat <- as.matrix(joint)

# Marginal P(Age)
p_age <- colSums(joint_mat, na.rm = TRUE)
p_age <- p_age / sum(p_age)


kable(data.frame(Age = ages, P_Age = as.numeric(p_age)),
      digits = 5, caption = "Marginal distribution of Age")

#
ahe_vals <- as.numeric(wage_df[[1]][-1])

numerator <- colSums(joint_mat * ahe_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
E_AHE_given_Age <- numerator / as.numeric(p_age)

# Part B 
cond_mean_tbl <- data.frame(Age = ages, E_AHE_given_Age = E_AHE_given_Age)
cond_mean_tbl <- cond_mean_tbl[is.finite(cond_mean_tbl$E_AHE_given_Age), ]

kable(cond_mean_tbl, digits = 4, caption = "Conditional mean of hourly earnings given age")

# Part C: Plot 
plot(cond_mean_tbl$Age, cond_mean_tbl$E_AHE_given_Age,
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Age",
     ylab = "E[AHE | Age]",
     main = "Mean AHE for each Age vs Age")
lines(cond_mean_tbl$Age, cond_mean_tbl$E_AHE_given_Age)
```

## Part D:

By the Law of Iterated Expectations,
\[
E(AHE)=\sum_{a} E(AHE \mid \text{Age}=a)\,P(\text{Age}=a).
\]

From the spreadsheet,
\[
E(AHE)=21.5106.
\]

Therefore, the average hourly wage in the population is approximately ~\$21.51.

## Part E:
The variance of average hourly earnings=
\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=E(AHE^2)-[E(AHE)]^2.
\]

Using marginal distribution of $AHE$,
\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=164.8203.
\]

Standard deviation of hourly earnings=
\[
\sigma_{AHE}=\sqrt{164.8203}\approx 12.84.
\]

## Part F:
The covariance between $AHE$ and Age is
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})=E(AHE\cdot \text{Age})-E(AHE)\,E(\text{Age}).
\]

From the marginal distribution of Age,
\[
E(\text{Age})=29.7663.
\]

Using  joint distribution of Age and AHE,
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})=5.7172.
\]

Covariance is positive, so higher age will be associated to higher wages per hour for this population.

## Part G:
The correlation between $AHE$ and Age is
\[
\mathrm{Corr}(AHE,\text{Age})
=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})}
{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(AHE)}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\text{Age})}}.
\]

So,
\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=164.8203, 
\qquad 
\mathrm{Var}(\text{Age})=8.1447,
\]
\[
\mathrm{Corr}(AHE,\text{Age})
=\frac{5.7172}{\sqrt{164.8203}\sqrt{8.1447}}
\approx 0.156.
\]

## Part H:
The covariance between age and average hourly earnings is positive, which helps us recognize through data that earnings tend to increase with age among workers aged 25–34. The correlation confirms a positive linear relationship between age and earnings. This relationship is visually supported by the upward-sloping pattern in the plot of conditional mean earnings versus age.
